nameStory: Rock sandwort gets its name from its love of rocky, sandy places where most other plants would struggle to survive. The word 'sandwort' comes from its preference for sandy soils, while 'wort' is an old English term simply meaning 'plant.' Think of it as nature's rock garden specialist!
description: Rock sandwort is a tiny, cushion-forming perennial that creates dense mats of narrow, needle-like leaves in rocky crevices and sandy spots. This diminutive plant rarely grows more than 2-4 inches tall, but can spread to form patches several inches across. Its small white flowers, each about 1/4 inch wide, peek out from the green mat like little stars. Despite its delicate appearance, this is one tough little plant that thrives where others can't.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms tight, cushion-like mats that hug the ground, with stems that feel slightly springy when gently pressed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, narrow leaves less than half an inch long that feel stiff and somewhat succulent, arranged in dense clusters along the stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with 5 rounded petals that feel papery-thin, blooming just above the leaf cushions on short stalks

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly from rock cracks or very sandy, gravelly soil where few other plants can establish

habitat: Rock sandwort specializes in the harshest spots - cliff faces, rocky outcrops, sandy shores, and gravelly mountain slopes throughout New England's higher elevations. Look for it wedged into cracks in granite ledges or growing from thin soil pockets on exposed bedrock. It particularly favors acidic, well-draining sites where competition from larger plants is minimal.

seasonality.spring: Small white flowers begin appearing in late spring, emerging from the dense green cushions as snow melts from rocky areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with clusters of tiny white flowers dotting the mat-like growth, most visible on sunny days when flowers open fully.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and tiny seed capsules develop, while the evergreen foliage remains green and identifiable in its characteristic cushion form.
seasonality.winter: The dense, evergreen mat persists under snow, often visible during winter thaws as dark green patches against light-colored rock faces.

funFact: Rock sandwort can live for decades in the same tiny rock crack, slowly building up its own soil from trapped debris and decomposing leaves - essentially creating its own garden plot one particle at a time!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with moss growing on rocks, but rock sandwort has true flowers and distinct individual leaves rather than the simple, scale-like structures of moss. Memory trick: if you can see tiny white flowers and needle-like leaves, it's sandwort - moss never has real flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Rock sandwort was recently moved from the genus Arenaria to Sabulina, so you might see it listed under its old scientific name Arenaria michauxii in older field guides. Both genus names relate to sand - 'Arenaria' from the Latin for sand, and 'Sabulina' from the Latin for sandy or gritty.
compareHints: Since rock sandwort is the only Sabulina species in New England, compare it with other members of the pink family like pearlworts (Sagina species). Rock sandwort forms much denser, more cushion-like mats and has relatively larger flowers, while pearlworts tend to be more sprawling with even tinier, less noticeable blooms. The habitat preference for rock crevices also sets sandwort apart from most other pink family members.
